title: Operators
description: Arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment/decrement, bitwise, shift, sizeof, and precedence.
objectives: Use arithmetic, relational, and logical operators
Use increment/decrement and the conditional operator
Use bitwise, shift, and sizeof operators

content.heading: Arithmetic, Relational, Logical, and Assignment
content.body: Arithmetic operators (+ - * / %) work as expected, with integer / integer truncating toward zero (7 / 2 is 3, and -7 / 2 is -3 in C99 and later, truncation toward zero rather than toward negative infinity). Relational operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) and logical operators (&&, ||, !) produce an int result: 1 for true, 0 for false (C has no true boolean type before C99's _Bool / stdbool.h's bool). && and || short-circuit, just as in most C-family languages. Augmented assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=, and bitwise equivalents) combine an operation with assignment.

content.heading: Increment/Decrement, Ternary, Bitwise, Shift, and sizeof
content.body: ++x/--x (prefix) apply the change before the expression's value is used; x++/x-- (postfix) apply it after — mixing these into a larger expression that also reads/writes the same variable elsewhere (e.g. x = x++ + ++x;) triggers undefined behavior, so such expressions should be avoided entirely. The conditional (ternary) operator, condition ? a : b, is C's compact if/else expression. Bitwise operators (& | ^ ~ << >>) manipulate individual bits; << shifts left (multiplying by powers of two), >> shifts right (behavior for negative signed values is implementation-defined — arithmetic vs. logical shift). sizeof(type or expression) returns the size in bytes of a type or variable at compile time — essential for correctly sizing memory allocations, covered in the Dynamic Memory lesson.

content.explanation: sizeof(int) reports the compile-time size of the int type in bytes on the current platform. 5 << 2 shifts 5's bits left by 2 positions, equivalent to multiplying by 4.

keyPoints: Integer division truncates toward zero; % gives the remainder
C has no true boolean type in C89 — relational/logical expressions produce int (0 or 1)
Mixing multiple ++/-- of the same variable within one expression is undefined behavior
sizeof(type) gives a type's size in bytes at compile time, essential for correct memory allocation
commonMistakes: Writing an expression that both reads and modifies the same variable via ++/-- multiple times, invoking undefined behavior
Assuming C has a real boolean type without including stdbool.h (C99+)
